summary: Defines a way to securely identify who sent a SIP message, which matters especially between domains. It adds an Identity header carrying a signature and an Identity-Info header pointing to the signer's certificate. It is a proposed standard. It was replaced by RFC 8224.

plainLanguage.summary:
The sender of a SIP request writes its own name in the request, and nothing stops it writing a name it does not own. This RFC lets the sender's own domain sign that name, so the receiving domain can check the signature.

The signature covers the important parts of the request, so it cannot be copied onto a different message without breaking.

questions: what is the sip identity header
how does sip identity signing work
subtitle: A signed Identity header lets a domain vouch for who really sent a SIP request.

tldr.problem: The From header of a SIP request can be filled in with anything, so impersonation is easy, and the security options already in SIP do not let a stranger check who sent a request.
tldr.mechanism: An authentication service in the sender's domain authenticates the sender, signs a hash of selected header fields and the body with the domain certificate, and adds an Identity header plus an Identity-Info header pointing to that certificate.
tldr.outcome: A receiving domain can verify the signature and know that the sender's domain authorized the From value. RFC 4474 was obsoleted by RFC 8224.

facts.label: Signature algorithm
facts.value: rsa-sha1, which every implementation must support

today: RFC 4474 was a Proposed Standard and has been obsoleted by RFC 8224, which is the specification to read for authenticated identity in SIP today.

sections.title: Why SIP Needs a Signed Identity
sections.content:
SIP (Session Initiation Protocol) lets a user agent, the program on a phone or computer, set up calls and other sessions. A request names its sender in the From header field, but whoever controls the user agent can fill that field in with anything at all, so impersonation is very simple today.

Many SIP services decide what to allow from an authorization policy. A presence service might compare the identity of a subscriber against a whitelist before accepting a subscription. An Internet telephone application might display the caller's identification, and a person might review it before answering. In both cases an attacker tries to get around the policy by impersonating someone.

The security tools in RFC 3261 do not close this gap well. Few user agents hold the end-user certificates that S/MIME needs, and Digest authentication needs a secret that the sender and the receiver already share. Chained trust through mutual TLS between proxies is weaker than an assertion that can be checked end to end. The P-Asserted-Identity approach only gives hop-by-hop trust inside a managed network of mutually trusting nodes, which does not fit wide Internet use.

This document defines an identity as a SIP URI, usually the address-of-record used to reach a user, such as sip:alice@atlanta.example.com, and lets the sender's own domain vouch for it. The scope is SIP requests; responses are left for future work.
sections.plainLanguage: Nothing stops a SIP request from claiming to come from anyone. This RFC lets the sender's own domain sign that claim, so the receiving domain can check the signature.

sections.title: The Authentication Service and the Verifier
sections.content:
The design adds two roles. An authentication service is a proxy server or user agent that holds the private key of a domain certificate. A proxy is the common choice, because a proxy usually has a stable hostname, a certificate, and access to the registrar functions that authenticate users in its domain. A verifier is the entity that checks the result. The two roles may sit in the same entity or in different ones.

The overview runs through one case. Alice, whose address-of-record is sip:alice@example.com, wants to reach sip:bob@example.org. She sends an INVITE over TLS to the authentication service proxy of her domain. It authenticates her, perhaps with a Digest challenge, and checks that she may use the identity in the From field. It then hashes selected headers and the body, signs the hash with the domain certificate, and puts the signature in a new Identity header. A companion Identity-Info header tells Bob where to get the certificate.

When Bob's domain receives the request, it verifies the signature and can conclude that the domain named in the From field authenticated the user and allowed that value. The same check can be done by Bob's user agent server.
sections.plainLanguage: Alice's own domain checks who she is and signs the request. Bob's domain checks that signature and the certificate it was made with. Both sides can then rely on the name in the From header.

sections.title: What the Authentication Service Does
sections.content:
The authentication service works in four steps. First it extracts the identity from the From field and, for a SIP or SIPS URI, compares the host part with the domains it is responsible for. If it is not responsible for that identity, it should process and forward the request normally, but it MUST NOT add an Identity header.

Second, it authenticates the sender and decides whether that sender may claim the identity. When the role is played by a proxy, it can challenge the request with a 407 response using the Digest scheme, or reuse the result of an earlier Digest authentication on the same TLS connection. A domain may apply its own policy, for example requiring the username in the Proxy-Authorization header to match the From field exactly, or allowing any of several URIs that map to one username. The check runs on the addr-spec of the From field; the display-name is not converted.

Third, it checks that any existing Date header is accurate. The RECOMMENDED maximum discrepancy is ten minutes, and a request whose Date is further out SHOULD be rejected. The service MUST also check that the Date falls inside the validity period of its certificate. Fourth, it forms the signature, adds the Identity header and then the Identity-Info header, and forwards the message normally.

The service must add a Date header and a Content-Length header if the request does not already carry them.
sections.plainLanguage: The service first checks that the request really comes from a domain it is responsible for. Then it authenticates the sender and checks that the sender is allowed to use the name in the From header. It then signs the request and forwards it.

sections.title: The Identity and Identity-Info Headers
sections.content:
Each of the two headers may appear only once in a message. Identity holds the signed digest: a quoted string of 32 hexadecimal characters, which is the base64 form of the signature. Identity-Info holds a URI from which the signer's certificate can be obtained, plus a required alg parameter naming the algorithm.

The signed value is built from a canonical string of parts of the request, joined by a vertical bar: the addr-spec of the From field, the addr-spec of the To field, the Call-ID, the number and method from the CSeq field, the Date field, the addr-spec of the Contact field, and the message body. If there is no Contact header, its place in the string is empty. If there is no body, the string ends with the last bar.

The only algorithm defined is rsa-sha1, and every implementation must support it. It is the SHA-1 hash of the canonical string signed with RSA, as described in RFC 3370, and base64 encoded as in RFC 3548. An RSA key of 1024 bits or longer must be used.

The URI in Identity-Info must dereference to the signer's certificate. Implementations must support HTTP and HTTPS URIs, and the resource must be of the form application/pkix-cert. Because the certificate at that address can change, the RFC asks for a new URI for each new certificate and for the older ones to stay available for longer than the likely lifetime of a SIP message, which it says an hour would most likely cover.
sections.plainLanguage: The signature is made from the important parts of the request: who it is from, who it is for, when it was sent and the body. Change any of them and the signature no longer matches.

sections.title: What the Verifier Does
sections.content:
A verifier works in four steps. It acquires the certificate for the signing domain, ideally from a cache indexed by the Identity-Info URI, and validates it following RFC 3280, checking that it has not expired, that the chain is valid back to a trusted certification authority, and that it is not on a revocation list. If the URI cannot be dereferenced it MUST return 436, and if the certificate cannot be validated it MUST return 437.

It then checks that the signer is authoritative for the domain in the From field. It rebuilds the canonical string and verifies the signature against it; if the signature does not match, it MUST return 438. Finally it validates the Date, Contact and Call-ID headers, and checks that the Date falls within the validity period of the certificate.

If local policy requires an Identity header and the request has none, the verifier sends 428, asking for the request to be sent again with one.
sections.plainLanguage: The verifier fetches the certificate, rebuilds the signed text from the request, and checks the two against each other. If they do not match, it sends back a message saying what went wrong.

sections.title: Security and Privacy Considerations
sections.content:
The signature covers more than the From field, so that a valid signature cannot be moved to a different request. The To field stops an Identity header being pasted into a request for another user. The CSeq field stops an INVITE being turned into a BYE. Verifiers must reject a stale Date, and the recommended window is 3600 seconds, and they must record Call-IDs from valid requests for at least that long, so the Call-ID acts as a nonce. Because a SIP user agent never generates the same Call-ID twice, a replayed Identity header is caught either by the Call-ID or by the stale Date.

The document is candid about the limits. The two headers cannot protect themselves, because an attacker can strip them. The display-name is not signed, since display-names are not unique. The Via header is not signed, because an attacker could insert a further Via after it, and the RFC says securing Via needs SIPS. An authentication service in the middle could alter a message before signing it, so users must trust their local domain. The correspondence between the domain in the From field and the certificate subject follows the procedures of RFC 2818, Section 3.1, and self-signed certificates should not be trusted without a prior key exchange.

For privacy, anonymous URIs with a valid domain can be signed, but anonymous.invalid cannot, because no authority for that domain can exist. Because the Contact field is signed, a privacy service cannot alter it after authentication without breaking the signature. The RFC also notes that the presence of a valid Identity header should not be the only factor in an authorization decision.
sections.plainLanguage: The seal also covers the date and a call identifier that is never reused, so a copied seal cannot be used on a new request or reused later. It cannot stop someone from removing the seal, though.
